summary.text: At \(n=140\), integer square bounds give \(\lfloor m\sqrt{5/4}\rfloor=156,160,175,180\) for \(m=140,144,157,161\), respectively, yielding \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). The claimed recurrence would instead require \(a(161)=528+484-471=541\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor,
\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating it at \(n=140\).

We first record an exact way to evaluate the square-root floor, avoiding any reliance on decimal approximations. For nonnegative integers \(n,k\), if
\[
4k^2\le 5n^2<4(k+1)^2,
\]
then
\[
\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=k.
\]
Indeed, all quantities involved are nonnegative. The left inequality gives
\[
k^2\le n^2\frac54,
\]
and hence, on taking nonnegative square roots,
\[
k\le n\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
Similarly, the strict right inequality gives
\[
n^2\frac54<(k+1)^2,
\]
so
\[
n\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1.
\]
Thus
\[
k\le n\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1,
\]
which is exactly the condition that the floor is \(k\).

The recurrence at \(n=140\) involves the four indices
\[
140,\qquad 140+4=144,\qquad 140+17=157,\qquad 140+21=161.
\]
We now compute the sequence at each of these indices.

For \(n=140\), take \(k=156\). The relevant exact integers are
\[
4\cdot156^2=97{,}344,
\qquad
5\cdot140^2=98{,}000,
\qquad
4\cdot157^2=98{,}596.
\]
Therefore
\[
4\cdot156^2\le 5\cdot140^2<4\cdot157^2,
\]
and the preceding criterion yields
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Consequently,
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(n=144\), take \(k=160\). We have
\[
4\cdot160^2=102{,}400,
\qquad
5\cdot144^2=103{,}680,
\qquad
4\cdot161^2=103{,}684.
\]
Hence
\[
4\cdot160^2\le 5\cdot144^2<4\cdot161^2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), it follows that
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(n=157\), take \(k=175\). Direct calculation gives
\[
4\cdot175^2=122{,}500,
\qquad
5\cdot157^2=123{,}245,
\qquad
4\cdot176^2=123{,}904.
\]
Thus
\[
4\cdot175^2\le 5\cdot157^2<4\cdot176^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). Hence
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(n=161\), take \(k=180\). Here
\[
4\cdot180^2=129{,}600,
\qquad
5\cdot161^2=129{,}605,
\qquad
4\cdot181^2=131{,}044.
\]
It follows that
\[
4\cdot180^2\le 5\cdot161^2<4\cdot181^2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
As \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Consequently,
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

If the conjectured recurrence held for every \(n\ge1\), then at \(n=140\) it would assert
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
The values just obtained turn this into
\[
542=528+484-471.
\]
But
\[
528+484-471=1012-471=541,
\]
so the asserted equality would be \(542=541\), which is false. Therefore the recurrence fails at \(n=140\), and the conjecture is disproved.
